catalog_quote: With some notable exceptions, stress in a Korlai word remains on the same syllable as in the corresponding Portuguese word, although from Portuguese to Korlai the posttonic syllable disappears, a trait also shared with the creoles from Daman and Diu. Thus, Portuguese fa-ca ‘knife’, a-gua ‘water’, and bo-ti-ca ‘shop’ became Korlai fak, ag, and butïk respectively. Consequently, Korlai words may end in /p, b, t, d, k, g, j/ and /ʣ/. In disyllabic words, Korlai generally follows a syllable-final stress rule. With trisyllabic words, the situation is more complex: those having a closed penult syllable (e.g. kom-bár-sa ‘speak’) have penult stress, but trisyllabic words with an open penult syllable show variable stress (e.g. us-ká-se or us-ka-sé ‘forget’ e-kó-tra or e-ko-trá ‘find’).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote confirmed verbatim in the held APiCS survey text at the stated section. (2) The deciding source is a 2013 grammar sketch by the principal (effectively sole) describer of Korlai, summarizing his 1996 Benjamins monograph; Glottolog lists only three descriptive refs, all by Clements, and API searches (Semantic Scholar, Crossref) surfaced no phonology article, instrumental study or dissertation on Korlai prosody. So the sketch is authoritative in authorship but second-best in depth: the 1996 monograph's phonology chapter (pp. 59-98) is the best available description and is not held (paywalled). (3) Open items fetched sources: Clements 2009 JPL (open) is silent on stress; Persée (Études Créoles 1997 piece, which appears to be Chaudenson's review of Clements 1996) and Brill (JLC 2015, sociohistorical) were bot-blocked and are not stress sources anyway.
